title: Short Stuff: History of English
summary: Short Stuff episode giving a brief history of the English language. The hosts trace English from Roman-era Britain (Latin among Romans, Celtic among Britons) to the Germanic invasions by the Angles, Saxons and Jutes, who brought North Sea Germanic that became Old English (c. 450 to 1100 CE). Legendary leaders Hengist and Horsa are mentioned as possibly the first English speakers. After the 1066 Norman conquest by William the Conqueror, French became the language of the royal court and upper classes while lower classes kept Old English, leading to Middle English with many French loanwords. The Great Vowel Shift in late Middle English changed vowel pronunciation. Early modern English was standardized through printing and the London dialect, and late modern English absorbed words from the British Empire such as bandana from India. The hosts discuss Caedmon, the illiterate monk-poet, and Bede, who recorded his story, and read a few lines of Caedmon's Old English poem. Sponsor/credit read at the end.

segments.title: Opening and introduction
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the short episode on the history of the English language and credit English Club, The Conversation, and Professor Ad Putter of the University of Bristol.

segments.title: Roman departure and Germanic invasion
segments.summary: After the Romans left Britain as their empire crumbled, Celtic-speaking Britons remained, but Angles, Saxons and Jutes from northern Germany/Denmark invaded and brought North Sea Germanic, the basis of Old English (roughly 450 to 1100 CE).

segments.title: Hengist and Horsa and the first English speakers
segments.summary: Legend says the Germanic leaders Hengist and Horsa were invited in to help protect the country, and may be considered among the first English speakers, though the story is uncertain.

segments.title: Norman conquest and French influence
segments.summary: In 1066 William the Conqueror, Duke of Normandy, took England; the royal court and upper classes spoke French while lower classes kept Old English, a class division that led to Middle English with many French loanwords such as sausage.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before discussing Middle English pronunciation.

segments.title: Middle English, Chaucer and the Great Vowel Shift
segments.summary: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales is in Middle English, not Old English. Late in the Middle English period the Great Vowel Shift changed vowel sounds, for example 'shape' becoming 'sheep'; linguists are still unsure why it happened.

segments.title: Early modern English, printing and British Empire loanwords
segments.summary: Printing and cheap books led to standardization around the London dialect, which became the basis of the first English dictionary and early modern English. Later, the British Empire brought in words such as bandana from India in late modern English.

segments.title: Caedmon, Bede and Old English poetry
segments.summary: Caedmon, an illiterate monk, is considered the first English poet; the monk Bede recorded his story. The hosts read the opening lines of his Old English poem, with 'modge bunk' (plan) as a highlighted word.

segments.title: Closing banter and credits
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the University of Bristol mascot and sign off with the show credit.
